questions.question: What does a limit at infinity describe?
options: The value of $f$ at one finite point, irrespective of the particular case.
The largest element of the domain
The behaviour of $f(x)$ as the input grows without bound

questions.question: For $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to +\infty}f(x) = L$, what kind of number is $L$?
Which expression is a limit as $x\to +\infty$?
What happens to $x^2$ as $x\to-\infty$?
options: As $x$ becomes very negative, $x^2$ grows without bound

questions.question: Which domain condition is used for $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to +\infty}f(x) = L$?
options: The function must be defined only on $(0,1)$
There is $r \gt 0$ such that $f$ is defined only at $x = 0$

questions.question: What is true about limits at infinity?
options: A function may have different limits at $+\infty$ and $-\infty$
The limits at $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ must always be equal
Limits at infinity are always finite
Limits at infinity are never related to asymptotic behaviour

questions.question: For $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to +\infty}f(x) = L$, what must be true after choosing a suitable $M$?
For $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to -\infty}f(x) = L$, which implication is required?
Why is a finite interval of the domain not enough to define $\lim_{x\to +\infty}f(x)$?
options: The definition only uses the value at $x = 0$
The definition needs $f$ to be decreasing
The definition needs $f$ to be defined for all sufficiently large $x$
The definition needs the domain to contain no real numbers

questions.question: Which statement best captures the phrase 'asymptotic behaviour' in this context?
options: Behaviour only at a local maximum
Behaviour only for the first few input values
Behaviour far from any finite region

questions.question: A function satisfies $f(x) = 1$ for all $x \gt 100$. Which conclusion follows from the definition?
options: The limit at $+\infty$ cannot be finite

questions.question: A student claims that knowing $\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x) = L$ automatically gives $\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x) = L$. What is the best correction?
options: The two limits may be different, so this does not automatically follow
The claim is always true by definition, in every case without exception.
The limit at $+\infty$ cannot be real

questions.question: If $\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=L$, the line $y=L$ is a:
What is $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\dfrac{1}{x}$?
What is $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\dfrac{2x+1}{x}$?
If $f(x)=2$ for all sufficiently large $x$, what is $\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)$?
What is $\lim_{x\to+\infty}x^2$?
Why can a function have different limits at $+\infty$ and $-\infty$?
options: The two directions always mean the same inputs.
The two directions examine different tails of the domain.
A limit at infinity must be unique across both directions.
The function must be unbounded in both directions.

questions.question: A function satisfies $f(x)=3$ for all $x \gt 10$ and $f(x)=-1$ for all $x \lt -10$. Which statement follows?
What is $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to+\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)$?
options: The limit must be different at $-\infty$.
